items.title: Ben Sidran interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 15, 2023
items.q: I said to I think it was Herbie Hancock or whatever, like what was the influence of being with Miles... when Herbie Hancock for example got really famous back in the early ‘70s, one of the effects of that is it pulled him out of the pool. You weren’t hanging out with Herbie Hancock anymore.

ctx.x: I like that analogy of legs on a stool. I know, I think of Kenny Davern, the marvelous clarinet player. And he somehow made a living just being a clarinet player. Not — no studio work, he was in a big band for a very short time and he said no I’m not going to do that. And all the things that you’ve done — have they affected your questions that you asked during your interviews that you’ve done?

That’s funny, I think of it the other way around. All the interviews that I’ve done have really affected my playing in that the takeaway from so many of the people I’ve talked to is the first thing that people tell you which is be yourself, you know, if you’re trying to © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

sound like somebody else you’re doomed to be second best, they’re already doing it. So at some point I really settled into owning my playing and not worrying about whether it was I don’t know, authentically part of the tradition or — I stopped comparing my performance and the time I put in and my practicing — I stopped comparing it with my hopes and dreams from being a 13-year-old kid or whatever, and just accepted it, and that really came from conversations with all — I mean Miles Davis, Sonny Rollins, Art…
